messages.body_plain:
Hello!
My name is Ellery and I am graduate student at University of Arkansas.

I was given an old quail survey dataset to complete as a side project, and am analyzing the data using multi-season occupancy models.

I am interested in generating yearly estimates of psi for my data set. However, I am struggling to derive 95% confidence intervals for the projected estimates.

I saw in a very old thread from 2011, "colext: how to use the predict function", that there was an example on how to do this using nonparboot methods, but I was unable to locate it.

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Below is a copy of my code.

Thanks!
Ellery Lassiter

Here is a summary of the code:
#model
fm1<- colext(~ESHArea, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)

# psi across years
## non-parametric bootstrap CI
## model 1-ESHAREA

npb <- nonparboot(fm1, B = 1000)
n...@projected.mean #estimates
n...@projected.mean.bsse #SE's

##attempted similar syntax as parboot
#'2' (col) as margin gives a single set of CI values, but don't align with occ or unocc estimates
apply(n...@projected.mean, 2, quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))

#'c(2,1)' (rows & cols) as margin just prints the occ and unocc estimates, rather than provide CI
apply(n...@projected.mean, c(2,1), quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))

##is projected.mean actually the mean? could use SE to calculate CI if so...
lower <- n...@projected.mean-npb@projected.mean.bsse
upper <- n...@projected.mean+n...@projected.mean.bsse

# empirical bayes estimate of # sites occupied in each year
## including parametric bootstrapping to get CI's
## model 1-ESHAREA
#this works :)

NumOcc <- function(fm) {
  re <- ranef(fm)
  colSums(bup(re, stat="mode"))
}

pb <- parboot(fm1, NumOcc, nsim=1000)

pb_results <- cbind(pb@t0, t(apply(p...@t.star,2,quantile,probs=c(0.025,0.975))))
colnames(pb_results) <- c("num occ sites", "lower", "upper")
pb_results

_ _
Ellery Lassiter
Graduate Student | BISC
University of Arkansas
evla...@uark.edu

Hi all,
Related to Justin's previous question on this thread: What would you do if sites were irregularly surveyed by year (i.e., some were surveyed multiple years and others not, in an inconsistent fashion) and some years have a low number of sites that are not spatially representative? The data below show number of detections by year (out of 3-6 annual surveys) for each site. The count of sites surveyed in 2015 and 2016 is ~200 while only about 40 sites each were surveyed in 2018 and 2019. Furthermore, the 2018 and 2019 sites were done in an ad hoc, spatially clustered fashion (and had VERY few detections), so I don't trust that the "occupancy" measurement for those sites in those years represents "truth" for the whole region (but all points from all years, together, are fairly representative). Therefore, a stacked approach with a "year" covariate does not produce satisfactory results (i.e., separate occupancy estimates by year are not trustworthy). Also, I'm not interested in changes in occupancy across years, just the overall effects of environmental covariates that may be driving occupancy.

Is a Bayesian approach with site (pointid) as a random factor the way to go to investigate factors driving occupancy?

Thanks,

Mike Allen
Rutgers Ecology & Evolution

Hi Ellery,

I'm not sure why the bootstrap isn't working for you, but you might take a look at the "colext" vignette for guidance. You could also try the new posterior prediction methods that Ken recently added. Here's an example:

library(unmarked)

vignette("colext")

example("colext")

## Empirical Bayes posterior distributions
eb.post <http://eb.post> <- ranef(fm)

## Empirical Bayes posterior predictions
sitesOccupied <- predict(eb.post <http://eb.post>, func=colSums,
                         nsim=1000)

## Histogram of predictive distributions
## You could pull the mode from this
plot(table(sitesOccupied[1,])) # year 1
plot(table(sitesOccupied[2,])) # year 2

## 95% CIs for each year
quantile(sitesOccupied[1,], prob=c(0.025, 0.975))
quantile(sitesOccupied[1,], prob=c(0.025, 0.975))

Richard

Hello!
My name is Ellery and I am graduate student at University of Arkansas.

I was given an old quail survey dataset to complete as a side project, and am analyzing the data using multi-season occupancy models.

I am interested in generating yearly estimates of psi for my data set. However, I am struggling to derive 95% confidence intervals for the projected estimates.

I saw in a very old thread from 2011, "colext: how to use the predict function", that there was an example on how to do this using nonparboot methods, but I was unable to locate it.

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Below is a copy of my code.

Thanks!
Ellery Lassiter

Here is a summary of the code:
#model
fm1<- colext(~ESHArea, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)

# psi across years
## non-parametric bootstrap CI
## model 1-ESHAREA

npb <- nonparboot(fm1, B = 1000)
n...@projected.mean #estimates
n...@projected.mean.bsse #SE's

##attempted similar syntax as parboot
#'2' (col) as margin gives a single set of CI values, but don't align with occ or unocc estimates
apply(n...@projected.mean, 2, quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))

#'c(2,1)' (rows & cols) as margin just prints the occ and unocc estimates, rather than provide CI
apply(n...@projected.mean, c(2,1), quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))

##is projected.mean actually the mean? could use SE to calculate CI if so...
lower <- n...@projected.mean-npb@projected.mean.bsse
upper <- n...@projected.mean+n...@projected.mean.bsse

# empirical bayes estimate of # sites occupied in each year
## including parametric bootstrapping to get CI's
## model 1-ESHAREA
#this works :)

NumOcc <- function(fm) {
  re <- ranef(fm)
  colSums(bup(re, stat="mode"))
}

pb <- parboot(fm1, NumOcc, nsim=1000)

pb_results <- cbind(pb@t0, t(apply(p...@t.star,2,quantile,probs=c(0.025,0.975))))
colnames(pb_results) <- c("num occ sites", "lower", "upper")
pb_results

messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users,

I am estimating the abundance of salamander larvae over a timespan of 11 weeks in five streams, with each stream having 30 pools (but I analyse these streams separately).
For this I collected replicated count data.

The following is an analysis of one stream with 30 pools ("30 sites").

My Null model is the following:
pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf1, K=t, se = FALSE, dynamics = ("trend"),
                  immigration = TRUE, mixture = "NB", control = list(trace = T, REPORT = 1))

To find K I wrote a loop, that loops through different K's.
It generates an Abundance list, as well as a list of the different K's with their AIC values.
Then I summed up all estimates from one model (Abun_sum).

Here is what I coded for the loop:

ks <- seq(150, 5*Kmin, Kmin/2) #Kmin = 54 (the highest value ever observed)
Abun <- numeric(0)
AIC_list <- matrix(0, ncol = 2)
colnames(AIC_list) <- c("K", "AIC")
for(t in ks) {
  m <- pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf1, K=t, se = FALSE, dynamics = ("trend"),
                  immigration = TRUE, mixture = "NB", control = list(trace = T, REPORT = 1))
  r <- ranef(m)
  a <- bup(r)
  Abun <- rbind(Abun, a)
  #isolate AIC value of model m
  K_AIC <- cbind("K" = t, "AIC" = m@AIC)
  AIC_list <- rbind(AIC_list, K_AIC)
}

#sum up all estimates from one model
j = 1
seq <- seq(30, 30*length(ks), by = 30)
Abun_s <- numeric(0)

for (i in seq){
  Abun_sum <- sum(Abun[j:i,])
  Abun_s <- rbind(Abun_s, Abun_sum)
  j = j + 30
}

This is the output of the AIC_list and the sums:
> AIC_list
       K      AIC
[1,]   0    0.000
[2,] 150 3252.709
[3,] 177 3242.215
[4,] 204 3234.455
[5,] 231 3228.494
[6,] 258 3223.826

> Abun_s
              [,1]
Abun_sum  8401.331
Abun_sum  9790.081
Abun_sum 11185.994
Abun_sum 12574.747
Abun_sum 13949.482

If I plot it it looks like this:

Then I tried to increase K even more...
And with the same model and code I got the following output:

> AIC_list
       K      AIC
[1,]   0    0.000
[2,] 260 3223.522
[3,] 270 3222.079
[4,] 280 3220.754
[5,] 290 3219.537
[6,] 300 3218.420
[7,] 310 3217.393

But with sums of:
> Abun_s
                   [,1]
Abun_sum 14050.63
Abun_sum 14554.98
Abun_sum 15056.67
Abun_sum 15555.63
Abun_sum 16051.78
Abun_sum 16544.85

This overall sum of abundance estimates should stabilise somewhen with an increasing K. But this doesn't seem to be the case here.
(1) Does someone know why the abundance estimates won't stop increasing?
(2) Also, there is an increase in the second Abun_s output of 500 in each step. But the AIC value is decreasing by ca 1... This seems odd to me as well.

I don't know where to look anymore. I also checked my raw data and my unmarkedFram - everything seems to be fine.
This code worked fine with the other streams, but not with this one.

All thoughts are greatly appreciated!

Best,
Michelle

Hi Michelle,

It's also possible that the model just isn't a good fit to your dataset, at least for the stream in question (or not enough data) and the result is optimization problems that mean no realistic value of K is likely to work. These open population models can be pretty hard to get working. It might help me (or, more likely, others who know these models better than me) to understand why you chose the 'trend' model and immigration=TRUE in your specific case (biologically speaking). Have you tried other variations? It also might be useful to see a sample of the data from the stream that is causing issues, and perhaps from one where the model seems to work.

Finally, it would be useful to see what kind of SE estimates you are getting if you set se=TRUE, even if K is too low.

I wouldn't necessarily expect there to be much of a relationship between the estimated AIC and estimated abundance.

Ken

Hi Michelle,

agree with Ken. These models are hard to fit. They have certain assumptions, like the closure assumption, i.e. the population doesn't change between corresponding visits. And, if there is any variation between the visits due to other factors than the detectability, this between-visit variation will be erroneously explained by the N-mixture model as low detectability, so it will bias your detectability downwards... Might help if you add covariates for the detectability, if there are some reasonable ones, but the model might be even harder to fit then.

Also, you assume that these abundance values are too large, but ... sometimes it might not be the case. We had such experience in our Atlas, when we came to densities sometimes notably larger than those already published. And our conclusion was (with some support from experts) that the majority previous estimates in literature were underestimated because they didn't consider detectability properly. Of couse might not be your case but just to share our experience.

Anyway, with the results you've shown, I would definitely try to raise K until it stabilizes, just to see where it goes. Let it run over the weekend :-)

Best regards

Tomas

Thank you all for your suggestions!

@Ken:
I chose the trend model, because I don't want to model the recruitment term.
I only look at count data of salamander larvae in the water and I do not look at the adults. Since the larvae cannot reproduce and recruit new individuals, I did not want to include this recruitment term.
Therefore I chose dynamics = trend. Also, I chose immigration = T, because larvae can drift and can "immigrate" into another pool. So, if a pool goes extinct, drifting larvae can "rescue" a pool by immigration.

Dear unmarked/hmecology readers, my colleague Di Prosser is hiring a post-doc here at Patuxent. Please see info below.
regards
andy

Quantitative Ecologist
Summary:
Dr. Diann Prosser’s Lab of the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center is searching for a highly motivated and talented quantitative researcher or statistician to work on a suite of ecology, spatial modeling, and avian disease research.  This position will consist primarily of quantitative modeling and statistical consulting focusing on animal movement analyses, wildlife disease prevalence and risk modeling, as well as distribution, forecasting and ensemble modeling. There may be opportunities to participate in field work, although this is not a focus of this position. The Patuxent Wildlife Research Center is a world-renowned research institution located within 30 minutes of Annapolis, Baltimore, and Washington, D.C.

Types of services required:  Examples of potential working tasks include designing and/or performing analyses on a variety of datasets including wild bird satellite, GSM, and nanotag telemetry data; creating ensemble models to assess risk of zoonotic disease emergence from wild to domestic populations including avian influenza viruses; waterbird population modeling; and agent based modeling with wildlife disease applications. In addition to the main projects included in this position, the successful applicant will be asked to regularly consult on analytical methods for previously collected data as well as the design of new studies. Co-authorship on publications is encouraged. Proficiency in R is essential, with experience in ArcGIS being beneficial. The candidate must be willing to assist with various projects other than those mentioned above, as this lab works on a variety of topics.

Required expertise/skills:
The ideal candidate has a doctoral degree in Ecology, Wildlife Biology, Statistics, Natural Resources, GIS, Mathematics, or a related field.   Experience with both frequentist and Bayesian methods is required, as is demonstrated proficiency with a wide breadth of analytical methods for ecological analyses. Candidates with Spatial, Movement Ecology, Forecasting, Machine Learning, and High Performance Computing experience is a plus. The candidate must be highly motivated and able to work independently, as well as have strong capacity to communicate well with the team.

Principal Duty Station:  This position will be based at the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, 12100 Beech Forest Road, Laurel, MD 20705 and is contracted through Natural Systems Analysts, Inc.  Start date is flexible depending on top candidate, however, January 2021 is desired. Given COVID-19 restrictions, some flexibility will be given to remote start date versus on-site. Salary is approximately $59K with benefits. The position is funded for 1 year with potential for 3-4 years depending on performance and fund availability.
How to apply:   Send the following to Dr. Prosser’s Lab at pwrc_app...@usgs.gov with “Quantitative Ecologist” in the Subject header: Cover letter, CV, writing sample, and 3 references in a SINGLE Word or PDF document titled with your name (eg. JohnDoe.doc or JaneSmith.pdf).  Closing date is December 3, 2020; however, applications will be reviewed as received and the position will be filled as soon as a highly qualified candidate is identified.

Elicia,

For your first question, backTransform() can't handle occuMulti output since there are more than 2 possible occupancy states. If you just call predict() on your model, e.g.

predict(fit, type='state')

You will get occupancy probabilities for each possible state (0000, 1000, 1100, etc.) at each possible site (taking into account each site's covariate values) along with standard errors. I think that's what you're after? This will still work if you don't have site-level covariates, you'll still get occupancy probabilities for each state and site, each site will just have the same predicted occupancy values as the other sites.

I'm not sure I  understand your second question. The code you shared should generate conditional occupancy probabilities for Coyote based on wolf status at each of your sites, given the specific set of site covariate values at each site. Maybe you are asking about calculating conditional occupancy probability for a specific set of site covariate values that aren't necessarily associated with any one site? If so you can use the `newdata` argument to predict(), supplying to newdata a data frame containing one row per probability you want to calculate and one column for each site covariate included in your model corresponding to those probabilities.

Ken
